# Overview
This document summarises the analyses done in R to support the Broughton Local Seaweed Services Model (LSSM) (aka *"Models, mesocosms, and field work to assess kelp mitigation of ocean acidification and hypoxia"*). 

Relevant aspects include the marine characterisation, the growth of kelp, and the estimation of the effect of kelp forests on the local ocean chemistry. As a fundamental aspect of this project is the iterative development of the model, we first developed a proof-of-concept model by combining example data with parameters from the literature. The proof-of-concept is intended to show that the proposed simulation is tractable within the scope envisioned for the work. We then upgraded the proof-of-concept to a more accurate and defensible working prototype by making the individual model components more realistic, and parameterising them with with *in situ* data collected as part of this project. 

# Model assumptions

- Kelp growth and its effect on DIC will (eventually) be modelled at an hourly resolution. 
- OA effects and mixing for the box models will be estimated using a temporal resolution defined by the tidal cycle. 
- Uniform mixing within the boxes of the box model.

# Methods
## Marine characterisation
To understand how kelp growth my influence ocean acidification, we needed to start with a reasonable description of the marine environment. For the proof-of-concept, we used available oceanographic data for the region, and upgraded the prototype using data collected for purpose as part of this project. There has been considerable work in the region over the last few years, including as part of the Broughton Archipelago Transition Initiative (BATI) and the Marine Planning Partnership (MaPP). Some of the mooring and field sampling data from these program relevant to this work (Figure 1).

### Temperature and salinity
BATI has 2023 data from 8 moorings in the region. Main ones of interest to this project are B5, in Blackfish Sound, and B7, in a sheltered location west of Gilford Island. The BATI moorings include a variety of sensors at different depths: 0.5 m = StarOddi CTD (T/S); 1.5 and 3 m = Hobo (T and Light); Bottom = T (Hobo). These data have been processed by Romina into a workable file of surface T/S (ctd_surface_cond_moorings2023.csv). T at depth from the Hobo sensors are contained in a separate file. 

MAPP has 5 moorings in the area. Of interest may be M5 (in QCS) and M4 (at the entrance to Knight Inlet). The MAPP moorings collect only surface (~ 1 m) T/S. These data have not yet been processed.

Environmental button loggers (T only) are distributed around the region and have been collecting data since 2022. Currently unclear on the number and locations, but could be useful for estimating spatial and temporal variance in T. Finally, T/S profiles were collected during kelp sampling work in 2023. However, as these are only point estimates, it's not clear how they could be leveraged for this study. 

### Light
Light data from the Hobos are challenging because the sensors foul up, and thus require regular cleaning. The data are available but need to be cleaned for the attenuation of light levels due to fouling. An algorithmic approach would seem to be warranted, along with a decision of when and whether to cull or correct the data. This work is pending, thus the light measurements are unlikely to be available for this work. 

We therefore simulated a Daily Light Integral (DLI) for our proof-of-concept model. DLI is a measure of the total amount of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) received over a day. We first calculate PAR in units of *(µmol photons m$^{-2}$ s$^{-2}$)*. PER HOUR? This was developed with support from ChatGPT. The photoperiod is simulated hourly for a year to match the DEB. DLI is related to PAR as (PARavg X photoperiod / 10$^6$). So in our case, we just need daily averages over 10$^6$ (things converts µmoles to moles giving DLI in *(µmol photons m$^2$ day$^{-1}$*).

**Currently can't match Pontier's DLI values without a fudge factor. Check PAR function first.**

### Alkalinity
Alkalinity is needed to calculate pH. Fortunately, it has a strong relationship with salinity. BATI moorings have salinity, so can get TA from salinity relationship. This has been derived by Evans for various locations in the eastern Pacific. For example:

\tab TA = 48.771 * S + 606.23 $\mu{mol}/kg^{-1}$ (Evans et al. 2015, for SE Ak)  
\tab TA = 59.88  * S + 278.79 $\mu{mol}/kg^{-1}$ (Evans et al. 2019, for the Northern Salish Sea)  

The fit is tight (r$^2$ = 0.94, root mean square error = 17.21 $\mu{mol}/kg^{-1}$, and was calculated using only salinity data < 33.6.

### Ocean carbon 
For our proof-of-concept model, we obtained pCO$_2$ measures from the Alaska Marine Highway System M/V Columbia during 135 service route transits between October 2017 and October 2019. Underway surface water measurements were collected as the Columbia sailed south from Ketchikan every Wednesday, arrived in Bellingham on Friday, returned to Ketchikan on Sunday. Measurements of temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen content, and CO$_2$ partial pressure were made every 2 mins on seawater drawn into the vessel from a ~2 m intake. A subset of these data were extracted for the southeastern portion of Queen Charlotte Strait, adjacent to our area of interest (i.e., between 50.6 and 50.7N, and -126.7 and -126.8W). This yielded 676 time stamped records that included T, S, and several different pCO$_2$ measures. These data formed the basis of our ambient, or kelp-unaffected water. We selected the value identified as "Surface Partial Pressure of Carbon Dioxide in Sea Water at Sea Surface Temperature" (SW_pCO2_wet_SST) for the proof-of-concept pCO$_2$.

Sample data for model development taken from Alaska ferry data. Accessible here:  
https://catalogue.hakai.org/erddap/tabledap/HakaiColumbiaFerryResearch.html  

For the prototype, we collected near-continuous measurements of pCO$_2$ along with ancillary measurements of temperature, salinity, and dissolved oxygen using two project-specific moorings. Each mooring included a CO2Pro, a star-oddi and a minidot for O2. Redundant star-oddis were attached partway through the season for groundtruthing. We also obtained direct measurements of pCO$_2$, total DIC (or TCO$_2$), and salinity from Water samples collected across time and space (see Figure X).   

## Kelp growth
### Proof of concept
We began by searching the literature for the available data on growth rates of bull kelp (*Nereocystis luetkeana*). Weigel and Pfister (2021) sampled kelp at peak biomass (June to Sept). They found:  
\tab Avg blade length             = 142+/-8.5 cm  
\tab Avg dry mass                 = 4.13+/-0.27 g  
\tab Scaled C fixing rate         = 2.35+/- kg C / m$^2$ * yr  
\tab Mean no. of plants per m2    = 7.66+/-0.86  
\tab Mean no. of blades per indiv = 41.5+/-2.95.  

The fixing rate is NET primary production, after accounting for the proportion C lost as respiration (0.27+/-0.08). Of this, 0.16 is estimated to be released as DOC (based on other studies - REFs). It is also based on a seasonal estimate of daylight hours (Apr-Sep) = 2617. The fixing was extended to an entire kelp forest based on the plant densities and blade counts above. However, the authors noted that earlier density measurements (plants per m$^2$) were lower, e.g., 2.25 (Foreman 1984), 3.7 (Barns and Kalvass 1993), and 4.57 Stekoll et al. 2006).  

For our POC model, we translated the fixing rate of kgC/m2/yr to a plant: 2.35/7.66 = 0.30 kg C / yr / plant. As a realism check, we converted the carbon fixed to wet weight using available conversion factors (dw = 0.13 * ww, from Bullen et al., and kgC = 0.25 kg dw) yielding an estimate of 9.23 (0.30/0.13/0.25) kgWW / yr / plant. Not unreasonable.  

This can be be further scaled to daily or monthly growth by disaggregating total annual daylight hours (Weigel and Pfister 2021). although this would assume uniform growth over the growing period. Nevertheless, further back-calculating kg C / frond, may help parameterise the scaling of the frond-based dynamic energy budget model (below) to a plant. 

For the POC model, we created a simple logistic growth model parameterised with the mature plant biomass (9.23 kgWW) estimated above.  

### Dynamic energy budget growth model
The dynamic energy budget (DEB) model developed by XXX is awaiting calibration for nereocystis by Barbosa. Our proposal relied on the completion of this model to provide a more defensible representation of kelp growth for the prototype model. The DEB parameters are  described in detail below to facilitate the eventual interpretation of the outputs. 

The dynamics of the DEB are represented by three state variables:  
\tab Mv (MolV)                     = the structural mass,  
\tab meN = MeN/Mv (molN molV$^-1$) = the nitrogen reserve density,  
\tab meC = MeC/Mv (molC molV$^-1$) = and the carbon reserve density.  
MeC and MeN are the masses of the C and N reserves.  

The DEB takes a table of [temperature, nutrients, dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), and light] as an input:  
\tab T =  K,          temperature  
\tab N =  molN/L,     dissolved inorganic nitrogen concentration  
\tab C =  molC/L,     dissolved inorganic carbon concentration  
\tab I = mol$^3$/m$^2$/d, photon concentration (= irradiance)  
  
The model returns a table of results for each time step. This table includes a few dozen parameters, with names that follow a standardised approach, summarised below [see DEB book]:  
\tab *j* represents a flux rate  
\tab *E* represents a reserve (or energy) unit, for either N or C  
\tab *M* represents molar mass  
\tab *V* represents the volume of the structure (i.e., frond) in L$^3$  
\tab *G* is the growth pool for a flux  
\tab *R* is the reproduction pool for a flux  
\tab *y* represents yield factors that couple flux processes  
\tab *t* as a suffix on the variable names, it represents the time step of the variable  
  
The following DEB outputs are assumed to be of use for assessing the effects of kelp growth on ocean chemistry:
Assimilation variable typical pathways:  
\tab j_NA = molN/molV/h,   uptake rate of N  
\tab j_CI = molDIC/molV/h, uptake rate of DIC  
\tab j_I  = specific relaxation rate  
\tab j_CA = molC/molV/h, DIC assimilation rate  
\tab j_Ot  = $O_2$ production  
\tab j_Ct  = Carbon (where?)  
  
Allocation to growth:  
\tab  j_EN_G = specific flux of N to growth SU (after maintenance)  
\tab j_EC_G = specific flux of C to growth SU (after maintenance)  
\tab j_G    = gross specific growth rate  
  
Total weight and length are closely correlated, as length is a species-specific function of biomass:  
\tab Wt       = g  
\tab L_allomt = cm, physical length  

Integration of results into the state variables for next steps:  
\tab M_V  = M_V + dMVdt * dt       The volume of the blade in terms of moles;  
\tab m_EN = m_EN + dmENdt * dt     The mass of the nitrogen reserve;  
\tab m_EC = m_EC + dmECdt * dt;    The mass of the carbon reserve  
  
Molar weights (g/mol) are used for converting moles (the mass unit in the DEB) to grams. These are listed in Lavaud et al.'s Table 2. The values for carbon and nitrogen reserves are higher than their atomic masses as they reflect the average molar mass for the compounds typically found in the reserve pool of kelps. Minerals and inorganics can also make up 15-25% of kelp's dry weight (DEB's typically estimate dry weight).  
\tab Molar weight of structure wV      27.51  
\tab Molar weight of N reserve wEN      17  
\tab Molar weight of C reserve wEC     30  

### Scaling considerations
From ChatGPT:

- A mature bull kelp (*Nereocystis luetkeana*) plant can have 30 - 50 blades  
- The stipe comprises 20-40% of the total biomass, depending on growth stage, season, and environmental factors.  
- A new sporophyte is typically a few mm to cm in length, and a few to 10s of mg (dry weight).  We began with a parametric model of growth.

We began with a 1-dimensional plant model. This quickly highlighted the need to consider the water volume "treated" by a kelp forest - a critical aspect of estimating the change in pH attributable to kelp. With the data described above, we used the carb() function from the seacarb package to calculate pH and other components of the carbonate cycle to estimate the change in pH attributable to kelp. 

## The box model

### Model assumptions
- Boxes are horizontally well-mixed and vertically uniform within each layer
- Advection and dispersion are parameterised, not dynamically modelled
- Vertical mixing is governed by stratification strength (e.g., Richardson number)  
- [for now! :] No internal feedbacks (e.g., biogeochemistry altering mixing)  
- External inputs are exogenous and time-varying (not coupled to internal state)  

### Physical state variables and properties
Each box tracks time-dependent physical state variables relevant to estuarine stratification and mixing: temperature (T, in C), salinity (S, in PSU), and water density (rho, in kg/m³), with density calculated at each time step using the UNESCO equation of state (rho = f(T, S)). These variables formed the basis for resolving both horizontal and vertical exchange dynamics. Optionally, additional state variables such as dissolved oxygen, dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), or nutrients (e.g., nitrate, phosphate) could be included, depending on the modeling objectives. The model also allowed for the calculation of light attenuation, vertical density gradients, and buoyancy frequencies to inform stability and mixing thresholds.

### Model structure and spatial configuration
For the proof-of-concept, we created a two-layer estuarine box model comprising 3 interior and 3 boundary boxes, each divided into a surface and bottom layer. This configuration allowed us to explore the mixing between the Village Sea basin, it's intertidal, and the adjacent, mixed waters of Knight Inlet. Box boundaries were defined according to bathymetry, and assumed hydrodynamics around mixing within and adjacent to the Village Sea. Table 1 summarizes the structural properties of each box, including depth and volume.

```{r, BoxVolumeTable, echo=FALSE, results='asis', escape=FALSE}

  Box_code <- c("VS_shore", "VS", "KI_M", "KI_F", "QCS"),
  Box_type <- c("Internal", "Internal", "Internal", "Boundary", "Boundary"))
  
  #...  Table should be made from what is loaded ... 
        
kable(name_table, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, 
  caption = "Box model physical structure") %>%
  column_spec(3, latex_column_spec = "p{4in}") %>% 
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"))
```



### Exchange between boxes
Horizontal exchanges include advection and dispersion. Advection describes bulk water movement (e.g., freshwater inflow, tidal exchange), while dispersion refers to tidal and wind-driven mixing across horizontal gradients. 

Vertical exchanges include Wind-driven vertical mixing and buoyancy suppression from stratification. These are modeled with a vertical diffusivity coefficient (K<sub>z</sub>), and are governed by advection-diffusion equations with mass balance over each box.

### Boundary conditions and external forcing
These apply time-varying inputs at the horizontal boundaries of the model and from the atmosphere. They should vary seasonally to simulate stratification and turnover. They can include:  
- River discharge (Q<sub>r</sub>) – freshwater inflow at the head  
- Marine exchange (Q<sub>ocean</sub>) – inflow/outflow at the mouth  
- Ocean salinity and temperature – for boundary boxes, and  
- Air temperature, wind speed, solar radiation – for surface heat and mixing. 

### Time integration and seasonal dynamics

The model is implemented using tidal time steps over a kelp growing season, and includes seasonal variations in freshwater inflow, thermal stratification, and vertical mixing. State variables in each box evolved according to first-order mass balance equations, numerically integrated using the `ode()` function from the `deSolve` package in R.  

Each scalar state variable (e.g., temperature, salinity, or oxygen) followed a generic advection-diffusion balance:
\[
\frac{dC_i}{dt} = \frac{Q_{\text{in}} C_{\text{in}} - Q_{\text{out}} C_{\text{out}}}{V_i} + \text{Mixing} + \text{Sources} - \text{Sinks}
\]

Where:
- \( C_i \) = concentration in box \( i \)
- \( Q_{\text{in}} \), \( Q_{\text{out}} \) = inflow and outflow volumes (m³/s)
- \( V_i \) = volume of box \( i \)
- **Mixing** = exchange due to horizontal or vertical dispersion
- **Sources/Sinks** = external fluxes such as air-sea heat transfer, gas exchange, or biological activity

Vertical mixing rates were dynamically adjusted based on stratification strength. For example, vertical diffusivity \( K_z \) was reduced when density differences between layers exceeded a critical Richardson number threshold.

Simulations were conducted using the `ode()` function from the `deSolve` package in R, with each box represented as a compartment whose state evolved through time according to these differential equations.

# Results

## Box model proof of concept
An initial set of 6 boxes was defined, with approximate areas measured. Two boundary boxes represented marine (WCS) and estuarine (KI) flows respectively. Volumes were calculated for surface and deep layers based on a mean depth, and an assumed surfaced mixed layer of 20 m.  

A flow matrix was estimated between the boxes ... 


- time step is one tidal phase
- flow matrices represent a nondimensional fraction of the source box volume exchanged per time step
- by incorporating DIC concentration, the matrix moves mass between boxes, using fraction of volume rather than absolute fluxes. This is consistent with tidal exchange models, and box models for fjords and estuaries (REFs). 

- alpha_mix specifies the rate of vertical mixing




## Marine characterisation

## Kelp growth
The DEB model takes a table (*grow_dat*) of [light, nutrients, temperature, and DIC] as input. Initial testing of the R <--> DEB connection was testing using a table with constant but randomized light, nutrients and DIC. The temperature was taken from the BATI5 mooring. The current DEB code (in LSSM_growth.R) successfully calls the DEB model executable **rundeb_KELP_p2.exe** compiled from MatLab code and passes it the gow_dat table. This leads to hourly values for all the parameters described in the DEB section above. 

Relevant calculations include:

Total C assimilated can be calculated using any of the following:  
\tab = sum of carbon assimilation per time step   
\tab = sum of assimilation rate * volume of kelp  
\tab = sum( j_CAt [molC/molV/h] * M_Vt [molV] ).  

This total includes the carbon used for growth and maintenance. The total fixed for growth is available as the sum of carbon used for growth per time step, or sum( j_EC_G [molC/molV/h] * M_Vt [molV] ). Subtracting this from the total C assimilated should yield the C used for maintenance, which is mostly released as respiration (i.e., DIC). 

Next step is to examine the version of this model parameterised for Nereo. This tasks is pending with Barbosa, and may be completed by mid 2025. Along with this it will be necessary to estimate total plant size from frong growth. This would include using below-bulb stype diameter to estimate stipe mass, plus some number of fronds to multiply by the growth value. (These fronds will need to be shed at some rate ... see Canvin et al. (2024).

Can we assume that the growth of the entire plant follows the growth rate of a blade? Not exactly according to Pontier et al. 2024.
